chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara, who said:

I asked him, 'Is there a Zakat upon the one who accepts Zakat?' He said, 'As for the one who accepts Zakat of wealth, then upon him is the Zakat of Fitrah, and there is no Fitrah upon the one who accepts Fitrah.'

So all these narrations indicate that the needy person and the one who is not of wealth, the Fitrah is not obligatory upon him. And everything that has come regarding that Fitrah is obligatory upon him, it has come by way of recommendation and preference, rather than obligation and compulsion.
So among what is narrated in that regard is what is narrated:

key_terms.الزَّكَاةُ: Zakat (alms-tax), specifically referring to the distribution of wealth to the poor
key_terms.النَّدْبُ: Recommendation, a legal status between obligation and preference
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابُ: Preference/Desirability, a legal status indicating a recommended but not compulsory act
key_terms.الْفِطْرَةُ: Fitrah (Zakat al-Fitr), the obligatory charity given at the end of Ramadan
key_terms.الْمُحْتَاجَ: The needy person, one who lacks sufficient wealth
key_terms.زَكَاةُ الْمَالِ: Zakat of wealth, the annual tax on accumulated assets

ai.seo_question: Is Zakat al-Fitr obligatory for the poor and needy in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Zurara clarifies that accepting Zakat (wealth tax) exempts one from the obligatory payment of Fitrah, whereas accepting Fitrah does not incur a second obligation, establishing a clear distinction between the two forms of charity. This hadith is pivotal in Shia jurisprudence for determining that Fitrah is generally obligatory only on those with surplus wealth, while for the needy, it is recommended (mandub) rather than strictly mandatory (wajib). The text further notes that other narrations imposing Fitrah on the poor should be understood as encouraging rather than compulsory.
